YOUR FIRST SHIFT

A calmer first game.

Start with the job. Then learn the buttons. A practical introduction for hockey clock volunteers.

Before the gameDuring playPenaltiesPeriod lengthsFirst-shift checklist

Before you touch the clock.

  1. Confirm the game format. Ask for the period and warm-up lengths, stop-time or running-time rules, timeout entitlement, overtime format and the rink curfew.
  2. Meet the other officials. Agree who operates the clock, records goals and penalties, manages the doors and communicates with the referee.
  3. Identify the installed controller. Read its model label and compare the hockey insert. A scoreboard brand alone does not identify its controller.
  4. Check the setup with arena staff. Confirm the connection, home/visitor assignment, time display and horn. Never reset an active rink controller to practise.
Find my controller →

Watch the play, especially at a faceoff.

In stop-time hockey, start the clock when the puck is legally dropped. Stop it at the whistle. Keep your hand ready and your attention on the official, rather than anticipating the drop or watching the display.

Record a goal only after the referee awards it. Note the clock reading and confirm the team, scorer and assists with the scorekeeper. For a penalty, confirm the team, jersey, duration and any special treatment before entering it.

If you start or stop late, stop making further changes and tell the referee at the next safe opportunity. The referee decides disputed time; use the controller’s correction procedure to enter the instructed value.

Penalty basics.

These are introductory descriptions of Hockey Canada rules. Your competition may use specific adaptations; ask the referee how a penalty should be displayed and when a player may return.

PenaltyWhat the timekeeper needs to know
Minor / bench minorNormally two minutes of playing time. A qualifying opposing goal can end the eligible minor on the shorthanded team. Confirm which penalty ends; do not erase every penalty when a goal is scored.
Double minorTwo consecutive minor penalties, not a single major. Treat the segments separately when applying a goal-related release.
MajorFive minutes. A goal does not end it. Hockey Canada also assesses a game misconduct; the officials identify the substitute serving the time.
CoincidentalEqual-duration penalties assessed to opposite teams at the same stoppage. The referee applies the cancellation rules and identifies any remaining time penalty. Do not assume both should appear as manpower penalties on the board. Junior/Senior variations can differ.
MisconductTen minutes of playing time for the player; by itself it does not make the team shorthanded. Return is at the first stoppage after expiry. Track it as instructed, separately from a manpower penalty.
Queued / delayed startA third time penalty may wait while two run. The serving order matters. A delayed penalty signalled during play is a different situation; wait for the official’s assessment before entering it.

Never use the end of a visible timer alone to decide a player’s release in a complex penalty situation. Coordinate with the penalty timekeeper and referee.

References: Hockey Canada 2026–2028, rules 4.2–4.7 and off-ice officials, rules 5.5–5.7. Reviewed 25 October 2026.

There is no single minor-hockey period length.

Do not assume that the simulator’s 15-minute default is your league’s format. Confirm all three period lengths, whether the clock stops at every whistle, and whether a mercy rule changes the timing. Running time, curfews, warm-ups, shift horns and timeouts are separate instructions.
